claim: The parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family.
source: The parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family, which bind to IL-33, either suppressing (HpARI1 and HpARI2) or enhancing (HpARI3) responses to the cytokine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited throughout the manuscript (Osbourn et al., 2017; Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI family proteins bind to IL-33.
source: The parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family, which bind to IL-33, either suppressing (HpARI1 and HpARI2) or enhancing (HpARI3) responses to the cytokine.
evidence: Supported by previous structural and functional studies cited (Osbourn et al., 2017; Jamwal et al., 2023; Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 suppress responses to IL-33.
source: The parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family, which bind to IL-33, either suppressing (HpARI1 and HpARI2) or enhancing (HpARI3) responses to the cytokine.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figures 1-3 and previously published work (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI3 enhances responses to IL-33.
source: The parasitic nematode Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri secretes the HpARI family, which bind to IL-33, either suppressing (HpARI1 and HpARI2) or enhancing (HpARI3) responses to the cytokine.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro and in vivo experiments shown in Figures 2-3 and previously published work (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI2 binds to DNA via its first complement control protein (CCP1) domain.
source: We previously showed that HpARI2 also bound to DNA via its first complement control protein (CCP1) domain.
evidence: Previously demonstrated and cited (Osbourn et al., 2017), and confirmed in this manuscript by EMSA experiments in Figure 1.

claim: HpARI1 can bind DNA.
source: Here, we find that HpARI1 can also bind DNA, while HpARI3 cannot.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: HpARI3 cannot bind DNA.
source: Here, we find that HpARI1 can also bind DNA, while HpARI3 cannot.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: DNA-binding ability can be transferred through CCP1 domain-swapped chimeras between HpARI2 and HpARI3.
source: Through the production of HpARI2/HpARI3 CCP1 domain-swapped chimeras, DNA-binding ability can be transferred, and correlates with in vivo half-life of administered proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments with fusion proteins shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: DNA-binding ability correlates with in vivo half-life of administered HpARI proteins.
source: Through the production of HpARI2/HpARI3 CCP1 domain-swapped chimeras, DNA-binding ability can be transferred, and correlates with in vivo half-life of administered proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 3 comparing HpARI2 and HpARI3:2 fusion protein activities at different timepoints.

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind to heparan sulphate (HS).
source: We found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) also binds to the extracellular matrix component heparan sulphate (HS), and structural modelling showed a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) which could facilitate these interactions.
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration (Figure 4A), heparin-agarose pull-down (Figure 4B), cell binding assays (Figure 4C), and isothermal calorimetry (Figure 4D-E).

claim: HpARI3 does not bind to heparan sulphate (HS).
source: We found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) also binds to the extracellular matrix component heparan sulphate (HS), and structural modelling showed a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) which could facilitate these interactions.
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration (Figure 4A), heparin-agarose pull-down (Figure 4B), cell binding assays (Figure 4C), and isothermal calorimetry (Figure 4F).

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 have a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain that could facilitate HS and DNA interactions.
source: We found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) also binds to the extracellular matrix component heparan sulphate (HS), and structural modelling showed a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) which could facilitate these interactions.
evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold structural modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HpARI3 lacks a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain.
source: We found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) also binds to the extracellular matrix component heparan sulphate (HS), and structural modelling showed a basic charged patch in the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 (but not HpARI3) which could facilitate these interactions.
evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold structural modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A mutant of HpARI2 lacking DNA and HS binding has a short half-life in vivo.
source: Finally, a mutant of HpARI2 was produced which lacked DNA and HS binding, and was also shown to have a short half-life in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with HpARI2_pentaR mutant shown in Figure 6, which lacks DNA and HS binding and has reduced activity when administered 3 days prior to allergen.

claim: During infection, suppressive HpARI1 and HpARI2 proteins have long-lasting effects at the site of deposition due to DNA and/or extracellular matrix interactions.
source: Therefore, we propose that during infection the suppressive HpARI1 and HpARI2 proteins have long-lasting effects at the site of deposition due to DNA and/or extracellular matrix interactions, while HpARI3 has a shorter half-life due to a lack of these interactions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing DNA/HS binding correlates with in vivo half-life (Figures 3, 6).

claim: HpARI3 has a shorter half-life due to a lack of DNA and extracellular matrix interactions.
source: Therefore, we propose that during infection the suppressive HpARI1 and HpARI2 proteins have long-lasting effects at the site of deposition due to DNA and/or extracellular matrix interactions, while HpARI3 has a shorter half-life due to a lack of these interactions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing HpARI3 lacks DNA/HS binding and the HpARI3:2 fusion (with HpARI3 CCP1) has shorter activity in vivo (Figure 3).

claim: IL-33 is a pleiotropic cytokine.
source: IL-33 is a pleiotropic cytokine.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the subsequent citations about IL-33's diverse functions.

claim: IL-33 can act as a potent inducer of type 2 immune responses.
source: It can act as a potent inducer of type 2 immune responses, and genetic studies show a strong link between the IL-33 pathway and the risk of developing allergic asthma (Moffatt et al., 2010; Oboki et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited genetic studies linking IL-33 to allergic asthma (Moffatt et al., 2010; Oboki et al., 2010).

claim: Genetic studies show a strong link between the IL-33 pathway and the risk of developing allergic asthma.
source: It can act as a potent inducer of type 2 immune responses, and genetic studies show a strong link between the IL-33 pathway and the risk of developing allergic asthma (Moffatt et al., 2010; Oboki et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Moffatt et al., 2010; Oboki et al., 2010).

claim: IL-33 responses are important for induction of anti-parasite type 2 immune responses in helminth infections.
source: Likewise, IL-33 responses are important for induction of anti-parasite type 2 immune responses in helminth infections (McSorley and Smyth, 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited review (McSorley and Smyth, 2021).

claim: IL-33 is a potent inducer of IFN-γ and regulatory T cell responses.
source: Conversely, IL-33 is a potent inducer of IFN-γ and regulatory T cell responses, dependent on the cytokine's context, cytokine release mode, and the cell responding to the cytokine (Bonilla et al., 2012; Schiering et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Bonilla et al., 2012; Schiering et al., 2014).

claim: IL-33's effects are dependent on the cytokine's context, cytokine release mode, and the cell responding to the cytokine.
source: Conversely, IL-33 is a potent inducer of IFN-γ and regulatory T cell responses, dependent on the cytokine's context, cytokine release mode, and the cell responding to the cytokine (Bonilla et al., 2012; Schiering et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Bonilla et al., 2012; Schiering et al., 2014).

claim: IL-33 can have pro-allergic, pro-inflammatory, or anti-inflammatory activities.
source: Thus, IL-33 can have pro-allergic, pro-inflammatory, or anti-inflammatory activities, and modulation of IL-33 responses can have a range of effects.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the previously cited studies about IL-33's diverse functions.

claim: Parasitic helminths secrete an array of immunomodulatory proteins which tailor the host immune response to allow parasite persistence without immunopathology.
source: Parasitic helminths secrete an array of immunomodulatory proteins which tailor the host immune response to allow parasite persistence without immunopathology (Maizels et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by cited review (Maizels et al., 2018).

claim: Each member of the HpARI family consists of three complement control protein domains, CCP1-3.
source: Each member of the HpARI family consists of three complement control protein domains, CCP1-3 (Colomb et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI2 binds directly to IL-33, inhibiting the interaction between IL-33 and its receptor.
source: Our initial characterisation of the HpARI protein (later renamed HpARI2) showed that it bound directly to IL-33, inhibiting the interaction between IL-33 and its receptor (Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claim: HpARI2 binds IL-33 via interactions between the cytokine and the CCP2 and CCP3 domains of HpARI2.
source: Our recent structural characterisation of the HpARI2:IL-33 complex showed that HpARI2 binds IL-33 via interactions between the cytokine and the CCP2 and CCP3 domains of HpARI2.
evidence: Supported by cited structural study (Jamwal et al., 2023).

claim: A long loop in CCP3 of HpARI2 contacts IL-33 at a site which overlaps with the IL-33:ST2 binding site.
source: In particular, a long loop in CCP3 contacts IL-33 at a site which overlaps with the IL-33:ST2 binding site, thus inhibiting cytokine-receptor interactions to effectively block the cytokine (Jamwal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited structural study (Jamwal et al., 2023).

claim: HpARI2 can interact with DNA in a non-sequence-specific manner via its CCP1 domain.
source: We previously showed that HpARI2 can interact with DNA in a non-sequence-specific manner, via its CCP1 domain.
evidence: Supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claim: Truncations of HpARI2 which lack CCP1 cannot bind to DNA.
source: Truncations of HpARI2 which lack CCP1 cannot bind to DNA (Osbourn et al., 2017), while HpARI2 truncations lacking the CCP3 domain can still bind to IL-33 (albeit with lower affinity), but cannot block interactions between IL-33 and its receptor (Chauché et al., 2020; Jamwal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claim: HpARI2 truncations lacking the CCP3 domain can still bind to IL-33 with lower affinity.
source: Truncations of HpARI2 which lack CCP1 cannot bind to DNA (Osbourn et al., 2017), while HpARI2 truncations lacking the CCP3 domain can still bind to IL-33 (albeit with lower affinity), but cannot block interactions between IL-33 and its receptor (Chauché et al., 2020; Jamwal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Chauché et al., 2020; Jamwal et al., 2023).

claim: HpARI2 truncations lacking the CCP3 domain cannot block interactions between IL-33 and its receptor.
source: Truncations of HpARI2 which lack CCP1 cannot bind to DNA (Osbourn et al., 2017), while HpARI2 truncations lacking the CCP3 domain can still bind to IL-33 (albeit with lower affinity), but cannot block interactions between IL-33 and its receptor (Chauché et al., 2020; Jamwal et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Chauché et al., 2020; Jamwal et al., 2023).

claim: HpARI2 binds to genomic DNA and IL-33 within the nucleus of necrotic epithelial cells, tethering the cytokine and preventing its release.
source: Thus, through CCP1-DNA and CCP2/3-IL-33 interactions, HpARI2 binds to genomic DNA and IL-33 within the nucleus of necrotic epithelial cells, tethering the cytokine and preventing its release (Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claim: HpARI1 blocks responses to IL-33.
source: Characterisation of the other members of the HpARI family showed that HpARI1, like HpARI2, blocked responses to IL-33.
evidence: Supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI3 binds to IL-33 but does not block interaction of IL-33 with its receptor.
source: HpARI3, however, bound to IL-33 but did not block interaction of IL-33 with its receptor.
evidence: Supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI3 stabilizes IL-33, amplifying responses to the cytokine in vivo.
source: Instead HpARI3 stabilised IL-33, amplifying responses to the cytokine in vivo (Colomb et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: H. polygyrus bakeri produces a family of structurally similar HpARI molecules with opposing physiological effects.
source: Thus, H. polygyrus bakeri produces a family of structurally similar HpARI molecules with opposing physiological effects.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing HpARI1/2 suppress while HpARI3 amplifies IL-33 responses.

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 can bind to heparan sulphate (HS) via their CCP1 domain.
source: Here, we investigated the role of the CCP1 domain of the HpARI proteins, and found that HpARI1 and HpARI2 can also bind to heparan sulphate (HS) via their CCP1 domain, while HpARI3 cannot.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple binding assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Extracellular matrix binding extends the half-life of HpARI2 in vivo at the site of administration.
source: This extracellular matrix binding extends the half-life of HpARI2 in vivo at the site of administration.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing HpARI2 retains activity when administered 3 days prior to allergen, while mutants lacking HS binding do not (Figures 3, 6).

claim: HpARI2 suppresses the release of IL-33 measured by western blot due to its tethering function.
source: As shown previously, HpARI2 suppressed the release of IL-33 measured by western blot, due to its tethering function (Osbourn et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C and supported by cited study (Osbourn et al., 2017).

claim: HpARI1 showed a trend toward suppressing IL-33 release that did not reach statistical significance.
source: HpARI1 showed a similar trend which did not reach statistical significance in this experiment.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HpARI3 does not alter the levels of released IL-33 as assessed by western blot.
source: HpARI3 lacked this ability and did not alter the levels of released IL-33 as assessed by western blot.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HpARI1 only binds 50% of DNA in EMSA assays.
source: Interestingly, while HpARI2 effectively bound all DNA, HpARI1 showed a reduced DNA-binding ability, only binding 50% of the DNA in this assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantified from EMSA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The DNA-binding activity of HpARI2 is localized to its CCP1 domain.
source: The DNA-binding activity of HpARI2 was previously shown to be localised to its CCP1 domain.
evidence: Supported by previous work (Osbourn et al., 2017) and confirmed by domain-swap experiments in Figure 1F-G.

claim: HpARI fusion proteins show DNA binding directly related to the source of their CCP1 domain.
source: In EMSA experiments, these constructs showed DNA binding directly related to the source of their CCP1 domain, with HpARI3:2 lacking, and HpARI2:3 showing DNA binding (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA.
source: Therefore, members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA, the latter of which is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DNA binding by HpARI proteins is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
source: Therefore, members of the HpARI family differ in their ability to bind both IL-33 and DNA, the latter of which is mediated solely by the CCP1 domain.
evidence: Demonstrated by domain-swap experiments shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins represent useful tools to separate the DNA binding and IL-33 modulation effects.
source: The HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins represent useful tools to separate the DNA binding and IL-33 modulation effects of HpARI2 and HpARI3, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the fusion proteins shown in Figure 1F.

claim: HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses in vitro.
source: As shown previously (Colomb et al., 2024), in this assay HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses, while HpARI3 amplifies them (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A and supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI3 amplifies ILC2 responses in vitro.
source: As shown previously (Colomb et al., 2024), in this assay HpARI2 dose-dependently suppresses ILC2 responses, while HpARI3 amplifies them (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A and supported by cited study (Colomb et al., 2024).

claim: HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retain the amplifying or suppressing activities of their CCP2/3 domains.
source: The HpARI2:3 and HpARI3:2 fusion proteins retained the amplifying or suppressing activities of their CCP2/3 domains.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A showing HpARI2:3 amplifies and HpARI3:2 suppresses ILC2 responses.

claim: HpARI2:3 shows decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI2:3 EC50=21.5 ng/ml).
source: Small alterations in activity were seen when CCP1 domains were swapped, with HpARI2:3 showing decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 EC50=21.5 ng/ml), and HpARI3:2 showing slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HpARI3:2 shows slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
source: Small alterations in activity were seen when CCP1 domains were swapped, with HpARI2:3 showing decreased activity compared to HpARI3 wild-type (HpARI3 EC50=1.2 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 EC50=21.5 ng/ml), and HpARI3:2 showing slightly increased activity compared to HpARI2 wild-type (HpARI2 IC50=1.9 ng/ml, HpARI3:2 IC50=1.1 ng/ml).
evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HpARI2 and HpARI2:3 tether IL-33 and reduce its release when co-administered with Alternaria allergen.
source: As expected, HpARI2 and HpARI2:3 tethered IL-33 and reduced its release, due to their combination of IL-33 and DNA-binding activities.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HpARI3 and HpARI3:2 slightly increase levels of IL-33 in BAL, possibly due to binding and stabilization of the soluble cytokine.
source: HpARI3 and HpARI3:2 lack tethering ability, and slightly increased levels of IL-33 in BAL, possibly due to binding and stabilisation of the soluble cytokine in the absence of DNA binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in western blot data shown in Figure 2B, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: IL-33 tethering does not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses at 24 hours.
source: Unexpectedly, when the downstream response to released IL-33 was measured 24 hr later (Figure 2C), IL-33 tethering did not correlate with suppression of IL-33-induced responses: while HpARI2 suppressed and HpARI3 amplified eosinophilia, ILC2 activation (as measured by surface CD25 or cell size by median FSC), and IL-5 release (Figure 2D–H), HpARI2:3 could not suppress IL-33 responses despite tethering of IL-33 at the 15 min timepoint (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing IL-33 tethering at 15 min (Figure 2B) with downstream responses at 24 hr (Figure 2D-H).

claim: HpARI2:3 amplifies IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI3 despite tethering IL-33.
source: In fact, HpARI2:3 amplified IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI3, and tended to have increased activity compared to the HpARI3 wild-type protein.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2D-H showing HpARI2:3 amplifies eosinophilia, ILC2 activation, and IL-5 release.

claim: HpARI3:2 is capable of effectively blocking IL-33-dependent responses despite lacking IL-33 tethering.
source: Similarly, despite a lack of IL-33 tethering, HpARI3:2 was capable of effectively blocking IL-33-dependent responses similarly to HpARI2 wild-type protein (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2D-H showing HpARI3:2 suppresses eosinophilia, ILC2 activation, and IL-5 release.

claim: The model of DNA tethering of IL-33 by HpARI2 cannot fully explain the activity of these proteins.
source: Therefore, these data indicated that our model of DNA tethering of IL-33 by HpARI2 could not fully explain the activity of these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unexpected results shown in Figure 2 where tethering did not correlate with suppression.

claim: The altered activity of the fusion proteins could be due to their effective half-life in vivo.
source: We hypothesised that the altered activity of the fusion proteins could be due to their effective half-life in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the unexpected results, tested in subsequent experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: HpARI2 can suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen.
source: We administered HpARI2 or HpARI3:2 either 1 day, 3 days, or 7 days prior to Alternaria (Figure 3A), and found that while HpARI2 could suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen, HpARI3:2 could only replicate this suppression when administered 24 hr prior to Alternaria (Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3B-E showing HpARI2 retains activity at day -3.

claim: HpARI3:2 can only suppress Alternaria-induced responses when administered 24 hr prior to allergen.
source: We administered HpARI2 or HpARI3:2 either 1 day, 3 days, or 7 days prior to Alternaria (Figure 3A), and found that while HpARI2 could suppress Alternaria-induced eosinophilia and ILC2 responses when administered 3 days prior to allergen, HpARI3:2 could only replicate this suppression when administered 24 hr prior to Alternaria (Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3B-E showing HpARI3:2 loses activity at day -3.

claim: The in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain.
source: Therefore, the in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain, and the HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 counterpart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3 showing HpARI3:2 (with HpARI3 CCP1) has shorter activity than HpARI2.

claim: The HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 CCP1 domain.
source: Therefore, the in vivo half-life of HpARI2 is controlled by the CCP1 domain, and the HpARI3 CCP1 domain confers a shorter in vivo half-life than the HpARI2 counterpart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 3 showing HpARI3:2 has shorter activity than HpARI2.

claim: Extracellular DNA is present at very low concentrations in bronchoalveolar lavage at homeostasis.
source: As extracellular DNA is only present in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at very low concentrations at homeostasis (Curren et al., 2023), and is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria, we hypothesised that the HpARI2 CCP1 could have a second binding partner which mediates its long in vivo half-life.
evidence: Supported by cited study (Curren et al., 2023).

claim: Extracellular DNA is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria.
source: As extracellular DNA is only present in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at very low concentrations at homeostasis (Curren et al., 2023), and is released in response to stimuli such as Alternaria, we hypothesised that the HpARI2 CCP1 could have a second binding partner which mediates its long in vivo half-life.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Alternaria-induced responses.

claim: Other host and pathogen CCP domain proteins interact with extracellular matrix constituents such as HS.
source: As other host and pathogen CCP domain proteins have been demonstrated to interact with extracellular matrix constituents such as HS (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008), we hypothesised that this could be the case for the HpARIs also.
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008).

claim: HS addition results in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2 in gel filtration chromatography.
source: We first used gel filtration chromatography to assess the mobility of HpARIs in the presence or absence of HS. While HS addition resulted in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2, no shift was seen with HpARI3, implying a lack of HS binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No shift in gel filtration elution is seen with HpARI3 upon HS addition, implying a lack of HS binding.
source: We first used gel filtration chromatography to assess the mobility of HpARIs in the presence or absence of HS. While HS addition resulted in earlier elution of HpARI1 and HpARI2, no shift was seen with HpARI3, implying a lack of HS binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 can be pulled down with heparin-coated beads.
source: Likewise, HpARI1 and HpARI2 could be pulled down with heparin-coated beads while HpARI3 could not (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HpARI3 cannot be pulled down with heparin-coated beads.
source: Likewise, HpARI1 and HpARI2 could be pulled down with heparin-coated beads while HpARI3 could not (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HS is present on cell surface proteoglycans.
source: As well as being a common constituent of the extracellular matrix, HS is present on cell surface proteoglycans (Xu and Esko, 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited review (Xu and Esko, 2014).

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells in mouse lung.
source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind less to CD45-positive cells than to CD45-negative cells.
source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HpARI3 does not show detectable binding to any lung cells.
source: To assess whether HS binding could mediate interactions between the HpARIs and stromal cells, we added PE-conjugated tetramers of the HpARIs to preparations of naïve mouse lung cells, showing that HpARI1 and HpARI2 bind strongly to CD45-negative stromal cells, but less to CD45-positive cells, while HpARI3 did not show detectable binding to any lung cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry cell-binding assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HpARI1 has an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM.
source: Finally, to assess the respective affinities for HS, we used isothermal calorimetry to show that HpARI1 had an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM, while HpARI2 had a slightly higher affinity of 4.2 μM.
evidence: Measured by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HpARI2 has an affinity for HS of 4.2 μM.
source: Finally, to assess the respective affinities for HS, we used isothermal calorimetry to show that HpARI1 had an affinity for HS of 9.6 μM, while HpARI2 had a slightly higher affinity of 4.2 μM.
evidence: Measured by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No binding could be detected between HpARI3 and HS by isothermal calorimetry.
source: Furthermore, these experiments confirmed that no binding could be detected between HpARI3 and HS (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by isothermal calorimetry shown in Figure 4F.

claim: HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface in their CCP1 domains.
source: We next used protein modelling to understand the differential HS binding of different HpARIs. AlphaFold2 models were produced to predict the structures of the CCP1 domains of HpARI1, HpARI2, and HpARI3. This revealed that while HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface, HpARI3 lacks this charged surface (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold2 modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HpARI3 lacks a positively charged surface in its CCP1 domain.
source: We next used protein modelling to understand the differential HS binding of different HpARIs. AlphaFold2 models were produced to predict the structures of the CCP1 domains of HpARI1, HpARI2, and HpARI3. This revealed that while HpARI1 and HpARI2 contain a strongly positively charged surface, HpARI3 lacks this charged surface (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by AlphaFold2 modeling and electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HS molecules can dock to various locations across the positively charged surfaces of HpARI1 and HpARI2 CCP1 domains.
source: We next used molecular docking to predict the structure of the complex between HpARI1 or HpARI2 CCP1 domains and the extracellular matrix component HS. Docking experiments predicted that HS molecules can dock to various locations across the positively charged surfaces of HpARI1 and HpARI2 CCP1 domains (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by molecular docking experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and HpARI2 has a positively charged surface which acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged cellular components, including DNA and HS.
source: Therefore, the CCP1 domain of HpARI1 and -2 has a positively charged surface which acts as a non-specific binding site for negatively charged cellular components, including DNA and HS, but this binding surface is lacking in HpARI3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling (Figure 5) and binding data (Figures 1, 4).

claim: Five arginine residues in CCP1 of HpARI2 form the positively charged HS- and DNA-binding surface.
source: Electrostatic modelling of HpARI2 indicated that five arginine residues in CCP1 form the positively charged HS- and DNA-binding surface (Figure 5A).
evidence: Identified by electrostatic modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HpARI2_pentaR has identical IL-33 suppressive activity in vitro as compared to HpARI2 wild-type.
source: HpARI2_pentaR had identical IL-33 suppressive activity in vitro as compared to HpARI2 wild-type (Figure 6A), indicating its IL-33 binding was unaffected.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro ILC2 assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HpARI2_pentaR lacks binding to heparin.
source: As predicted, however, HpARI2_pentaR lacked binding to both heparin (Figure 6B) and DNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by heparin-agarose pull-down assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HpARI2_pentaR lacks binding to DNA.
source: As predicted, however, HpARI2_pentaR lacked binding to both heparin (Figure 6B) and DNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HpARI2_pentaR has a shorter in vivo half-life than wild-type HpARI2.
source: When HpARI2_pentaR was administered to mice prior to Alternaria administration, like HpARI3:2, it was found to have a shorter in vivo half-life than the wild-type HpARI2 protein (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6D-H showing loss of activity at day -3.

claim: HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein.
source: Taken together, this data shows that HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein, and that interactions with HS increase its in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the HS-binding data shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Interactions with HS increase HpARI2's in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
source: Taken together, this data shows that HpARI2 is an HS-binding protein, and that interactions with HS increase its in vivo half-life at the site of administration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing mutants lacking HS binding have shorter half-lives (Figures 3, 6).

claim: The prototypic Hp-TGM sequence has undergone selection to carry out a range of contradictory functions.
source: Thus the prototypic Hp-TGM sequence has undergone selection to carry out a range of contradictory functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing different Hp-TGM family members have opposing activities.

claim: The activity of the HpARIs is controlled by timing of release, in vivo half-life, and localisation within the host, controlled by interactions with the extracellular matrix.
source: As the Hp-TGM proteins are targeted to different cellular targets through co-receptor interactions, we propose that the activity of the HpARIs is controlled by timing of release, in vivo half-life, and localisation within the host, controlled by interactions with the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing HS binding controls half-life.

claim: The positively charged patch in HpARI2's CCP1 domain lengthens the effective half-life of the protein in vivo via binding to DNA and HS.
source: We show here that HpARI1 and HpARI2 have a positively charged patch in their CCP1 domain. In the case of HpARI2, we show that this charged patch lengthens the effective half-life of the protein in vivo via binding to DNA and, more relevantly, HS.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with HpARI2_pentaR mutant lacking the charged patch (Figure 6).

claim: Binding to the extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans prevents diffusion of HpARI1 and HpARI2, keeps the local concentration high, and prevents loss of protein to the circulation.
source: We propose that this binding to the extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans prevents diffusion of HpARI1 and HpARI2, keeps the local concentration high, and prevents loss of protein to the circulation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data showing HS binding extends half-life.

claim: HpARI2 is a more effective IL-33 suppressor compared to a systemically administered monoclonal antibody due to its extracellular matrix binding.
source: This makes HpARI2 a particularly effective IL-33 suppressor when compared to a systemically administered monoclonal antibody which must reach an effective concentration throughout the circulation of the host to allow blockade at the site of IL-33 release.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on the proposed mechanism of HS-mediated localization.

claim: Some cytokines and chemokines bind to the extracellular matrix to ensure their effects are constrained to the local milieu.
source: Some cytokines and chemokines (Ridley et al., 2023) bind to the extracellular matrix to ensure their effects are constrained to the local milieu.
evidence: Supported by cited review (Ridley et al., 2023).

claim: Abrogating the HS-binding activity of IFN-γ results in fatal systemic inflammation after viral infection.
source: This is critical for their activity: it was recently shown that abrogating the HS-binding activity of IFN-γ results in fatal systemic (rather than local) inflammation after viral infection (Kemna et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Kemna et al., 2023).

claim: Retaining proteins on the extracellular matrix is being developed for increasing the efficacy of protein-based therapeutics while decreasing toxicity at off-target sites.
source: This approach of retaining proteins on the extracellular matrix is being developed for increasing the efficacy of protein-based therapeutics, while decreasing toxicity at off-target sites (Alshoubaki et al., 2023; Martino et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Alshoubaki et al., 2023; Martino et al., 2014).

claim: Heparin binding prolongs the blocking of VEGF signalling by recombinant VEGFR1 in therapeutic use.
source: This was exemplified in a study showing that heparin binding was able to prolong the blocking of VEGF signalling by recombinant VEGFR1 in therapeutic use (Xin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Xin et al., 2021).

claim: Parasitic helminths have evolved the technique of using extracellular matrix binding to localise immunomodulatory proteins.
source: It appears that this same technique has been evolved by parasitic helminths to localise immunomodulatory proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing HpARI proteins use HS binding for localization.

claim: HS binding has been demonstrated for several other CCP domain proteins, including KCP, Factor H, and C4BP.
source: HS binding has been demonstrated for several other CCP domain proteins, including the viral CCP protein Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus complement control protein (KCP) (Mark et al., 2006), and the mammalian proteins Factor H (Schmidt et al., 2008) and C4BP (Spijkers et al., 2008; Trouw et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited studies (Mark et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2008; Spijkers et al., 2008; Trouw et al., 2005).

claim: C4BP presents a basic patch which is able to bind both DNA and HS, similarly to HpARI1 and HpARI2.
source: In C4BP, the protein presents a basic patch which is able to bind both DNA and HS, similarly to the data we show here for HpARI1 and HpARI2.
evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about C4BP, drawing parallels to the HpARI data.

claim: HpARI1 has lower affinity for DNA and HS compared to HpARI2.
source: While HpARI1 binds to DNA and HS, it has lower affinity for these ligands compared to HpARI2, and in the DNA-binding assays only bound to 50% of the total DNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA (Figure 1E) and ITC (Figure 4D-E) showing weaker binding for HpARI1.

claim: HpARI1 may remain partially in solution, diffusing further from the site of deposition than HpARI2.
source: It is unclear what the purpose is of this reduced binding affinity, but it could be that HpARI1 remains partially in solution, diffusing further from the site of deposition than HpARI2, and so mediating its effects at a greater distance from the site of release.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of HpARI1's weaker binding.

claim: IL-33 released by epithelial cells in the intestine induces a type 2 immune response which results in parasite ejection.
source: In parasitic infection, IL-33 released by epithelial cells in the intestine induces a type 2 immune response which results in parasite ejection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-33's role in anti-parasite immunity.

claim: IL-33 released by myeloid cells in helminth infection induces regulatory T cell expansion, suppressing effector immune responses and resulting in increased parasite burdens.
source: In the same helminth infection model, IL-33 released by myeloid cells induced regulatory T cell expansion, suppressing effector immune responses and resulting in increased parasite burdens (Hung et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Hung et al., 2020).

claim: At different sites and in different cells, IL-33 can have directly opposing effects.
source: Therefore, at different sites and in different cells, IL-33 can have directly opposing effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study (Hung et al., 2020) showing context-dependent IL-33 effects.

claim: HpARI2 binds strongly to the extracellular matrix and is retained in the local milieu of the parasite where it blocks IL-33 released in response to infection.
source: In the context of the findings outlined here, we propose the following model for the HpARI family's effects: HpARI2 binds strongly to the extracellular matrix, and is retained in the local milieu of the parasite where it blocks IL-33 released in response to infection.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing HpARI2's HS binding and long half-life.

claim: HpARI1 binds less strongly to HS and may diffuse slightly further from the site of deposition to block more distant IL-33 responses.
source: HpARI1 binds less strongly to HS, and therefore may diffuse slightly further from the site of deposition, to block more distant IL-33 responses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on HpARI1's weaker HS binding affinity.

claim: HpARI3 lacks HS binding and diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites, potentially amplifying IL-33-dependent regulatory responses.
source: Finally, HpARI3 lacks HS binding and so diffuses freely to amplify IL-33 responses at distal sites, which we hypothesise could amplify IL-33-dependent regulatory responses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on HpARI3's lack of HS binding and its IL-33-amplifying activity.

claim: Transgenic parasites deficient for individual HpARI proteins would be useful to investigate the proposed model but have proved intractable for parasitic nematodes.
source: To investigate these hypotheses, transgenic parasites deficient for individual HpARI proteins would be useful, however this has proved intractable for parasitic nematodes (Quinzo et al., 2022), and has not been achieved in H. polygyrus bakeri to date.
evidence: Supported by cited study (Quinzo et al., 2022) about difficulties in nematode transgenesis.

claim: Other parasitic helminths may have used extracellular matrix binding as a technique to retain immunoregulators within the local milieu.
source: The findings outlined here may be applicable beyond H. polygyrus bakeri, as it appears likely that other parasitic helminths have used extracellular matrix binding as a technique to retain immunoregulators within the local milieu.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings with HpARI proteins.

claim: Trichuris muris secretes the immunoregulatory protein p43 which binds and blocks IL-13 and has HS-binding activity.
source: Indeed, Trichuris muris, another intestinal nematode, secretes the immunoregulatory protein p43. This protein binds and blocks IL-13, but also has HS-binding activity which has been proposed to tether p43 to the extracellular matrix, increasing survival of the protein at the site of infection (Bancroft et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited study (Bancroft et al., 2019).

claim: H. polygyrus bakeri has developed a series of immunomodulatory protein families, including 10 Hp-TGMs and 2 HpBARIs.
source: H. polygyrus bakeri has developed a series of immunomodulatory protein families, including 10 Hp-TGMs and 2 HpBARIs, therefore it will be informative to investigate whether members of these families also bind to the extracellular matrix, and whether this alters their in vivo localisation and/or half-life.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H. polygyrus bakeri's immunomodulatory proteins.

claim: A novel HS-binding ability of members of the HpARI family increases their in vivo half-life and activity at the site of deposition.
source: In conclusion, we describe a novel HS-binding ability of members of the HpARI family and show that this binding increases their in vivo half-life and activity at the site of deposition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings demonstrated throughout the manuscript.
